citeAs: Paperno, Denis, Germán Kruszewski, Angeliki Lazaridou, Quan Ngoc Pham, Raffaella Bernardi, Sandro Pezzelle, Marco Baroni, Gemma Boleda, and Raquel Fernández (2016). The LAMBADA dataset: Word prediction requiring a broad discourse context. arXiv.
creator: Denis Paperno, Germán Kruszewski, Angeliki Lazaridou, Quan Ngoc Pham, Raffaella Bernardi, Sandro Pezzelle, Marco Baroni, Gemma Boleda, Raquel Fernández (University of Trento; University of Amsterdam)
description: LAMBADA is a dataset of narrative passages for a word prediction task in which human subjects can guess the last word when given the full passage, but not when given only the final sentence. It is designed to evaluate whether computational models can use broad discourse context rather than only local context.
name: LAMBADA
publisher: CIMeC - Center for Mind/Brain Sciences, University of Trento
rai:annotationsPerItem: At least 12 human judgments per candidate passage in the filtering pipeline: 1 subject on the whole passage at step 1, 1 subject on the whole passage at step 2 if step 1 was correct, and up to 10 subjects on the target sentence only at step 3 until the word was guessed or 10 unsuccessful guesses were reached.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: The paper reports filtering outcomes from the crowdsourcing pipeline: 84–86% of items were discarded at step 1, an additional 6–7% at step 2, and another 3–5% at step 3. The inclusion criteria were strict: two consecutive subjects had to exactly match the missing word using the full passage, and no subject out of ten could provide it from local sentence context alone, even with 3 guesses.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Candidate passages were evaluated by human subjects in three steps: first one subject guessed the target word from the whole passage; if correct, a second subject guessed from the whole passage; if also correct, additional subjects guessed from the target sentence only until the word was guessed or 10 unsuccessful guesses were reached. Subjects in step 3 were allowed 3 guesses per sentence, and the same subject was not allowed to judge the same item in both passage and sentence conditions.
rai:dataBiases: The authors state that using unpublished novels minimizes the usefulness of general world knowledge and external resources compared with news, Wikipedia, or famous novels. They also note distributional biases in the resulting dataset, including that more than 80% of passages contain the target word in the context, proper nouns are overrepresented, and quoted direct speech appears more often in LAMBADA than in input items.
rai:dataCollection: The dataset was built from the Book Corpus. After duplicate removal and filtering potentially offensive material with a stop word list, the authors randomly split novels into training and development+testing partitions, then built LAMBADA from the latter. Candidate passages were automatically filtered using language models to remove items likely guessable from local context, and the remaining passages were further filtered through a CrowdFlower human evaluation pipeline.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: The source data are unpublished novels from the Book Corpus. After duplicate removal and filtering potentially offensive material with a stop word list, the corpus contained 5,325 novels and 465 million words.
rai:dataCollectionType: Secondary Data analysis, Document analysis, Manual Human Curator
rai:dataLimitations: The paper notes that the inclusion criteria are very strict, requiring exact word matches from two subjects with full context and failure by up to ten subjects with local context only. Because of cost considerations, the authors could not use more subjects at stage 1, and they adopted a strict hit-or-miss approach rather than allowing plausible or synonymous continuations.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: The authors constructed passages by taking the minimum number of preceding complete sentences totaling at least 50 tokens as context and using the last word of the target sentence as the prediction target. They also automatically filtered out passages whose target word probability was at least 0.00175 under any of four language models before human filtering.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: The source Book Corpus underwent duplicate removal and filtering of potentially offensive material with a stop word list. Candidate passages were defined as a context plus target sentence, where context length was the minimum number of complete preceding sentences totaling at least 50 tokens. The novels were split into training and development/testing partitions, and passages whose target word had probability ≥ 0.00175 under any of four language models were excluded before human filtering.
rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is intended as a benchmark to evaluate language models on their ability to use broad discourse context for word prediction and natural language understanding.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: A combination of four language models was used to filter candidate passages before human annotation: a pre-trained recurrent neural network (RNN), a standard 4-gram model, an RNN, and a feed-forward model.
